Grade 4 · Unit 4.4

Structures, Senses, and Responses

How do body parts and senses help living things survive?

Every living thing is built with parts that help it survive. This unit covers the jobs of outside parts like roots, fur and beaks, the jobs of inside parts like hearts, lungs and plant tubes, and how senses gather information that the brain uses to guide a response.

In this lesson

  1. External structures have jobs
  2. Internal structures have jobs
  3. Senses send information and the body responds
  4. Try it at home
  5. Check yourself
  6. Play: Body Part Match

Concept 1

External structures have jobs

Outside parts such as roots, leaves, fur, beaks, and spines help organisms get needs, grow, and stay safe.

Diagram

Plant structures

roots, stem, leaf, flower.

“Roots hold and soak up. Leaves catch light. Flowers help make seeds.”

Real world

Cactus spines

a cactus with spines.

“Spines help protect the cactus. Structures help survival.”

Try it

Structure match

cards with structures and cards with jobs.

“Match the part to its job. Then argue: This part helps because…”

Concept 2

Internal structures have jobs

Inside parts such as hearts, lungs, skeletons, and plant transport tubes help organisms live, grow, and reproduce.

Diagram

Human inside

heart, lungs, skeleton.

“Your heart pumps blood. Your lungs take in air. Your skeleton supports you.”

Diagram

Plant stem inside

a stem with tiny tubes.

“Stems carry water and sugar inside the plant.”

Try it

Inside/outside sort

structure cards sorted into inside and outside groups.

“Sort inside and outside. Then ask: What job does it do?”

Data

Argument frame

sentence frame: “I claim ___ helps survival because ___.”

“Pick one inside structure. Use evidence.”

Concept 3

Senses send information and the body responds

Sense organs collect information, the brain processes it, and the body responds.

Try it

Ruler-drop reaction

one student holding a ruler, another student catching it when it drops. The dropper waits a different secret time each try, so the catcher cannot guess when it will fall.

“Your eye sees the drop. Your brain says catch. Your hand moves.”

Diagram

Path model

eye or ear → brain → muscles.

“Information goes in. The brain sends a response.”

Real world

Deer hears predator

a deer with ears up.

“A deer hears a sound. Its brain says danger. It runs.”

Data

Reaction data

catch marks on ruler for three trials, plus provided dataset.

“Record your catch marks. Provided dataset: sight 12 cm, 10 cm, 9 cm; sound cue 14 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm. The farther down the ruler you catch it, the slower you were.”

The sound cue depends on when the dropper says “now,” so sight versus sound is a rough comparison. Swap roles and see if it holds.

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Fair-test investigation: “Which sense gives a quicker response: sight or sound?” Students compare two ways to start the catch: watching the ruler with eyes open, and eyes closed with a sound cue (the dropper says “now” at the instant of release). The same two students keep ruler height and hand position the same, the dropper waits a different secret time before each drop, and they test three trials each. They record catch marks and write one claim with evidence. The sound cue depends on how well the dropper times the word, so they say it is a rough comparison, then swap roles and see whether the result holds.

Try it

What you need

ruler, paper, index cards, tape, crayons, pictures of plants and animals, string optional.

Safety: drop only light rulers; keep feet clear. If using real leaves, soil, or outdoor samples, wash hands afterward.

What you do

Sort external and internal structures. Match structures to jobs. Build a sense→brain→response model. Test reaction distance with a ruler drop.

Words to know

structure
a part with a job.
external
outside.
internal
inside.
sense
a way the body collects information, such as sight or hearing.
brain
organ that processes information.
response
what the body does after processing information.
organ
a body part with a special job.
survival
staying alive.
model
a drawing or tool that shows how something works.
evidence
observations that support a claim.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Only outside body parts matter.” Correct: internal structures have jobs too.
  • “Plant parts are just decorations.” Correct: plant structures help survival, growth, and reproduction.
  • “Plant parts are not real structures.” Correct: roots, stems, leaves, and flowers are structures with jobs.
  • “Responses happen without information.” Correct: senses collect information, the brain processes it, and the body responds.
  • “Senses and responses are the same thing.” Correct: senses collect information; responses are actions after processing.
  • “The brain is not part of the body’s response system.” Correct: the brain processes information and helps the body respond.

Limits and cautions:

  • Internal structures are simplified; cells and organ systems are not taught here. Those belong in later units.
  • Ruler-drop distance is evidence of reaction time, not an exact time measurement. The sound-cue version also depends on the dropper’s timing, so it is a rough comparison, and the unit says so.
  • Plant internal transport is simplified; the unit avoids xylem/phloem detail.
  • The unit does not cover inherited traits or ecosystems; those are in 3.3, 3.4, and 5.3.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 4-LS1-1: Construct an argument that plants and animals have internal and external structures that support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction.
  • 4-LS1-2: Use a model to describe that animals receive information through their senses, process it in their brain, and respond to it.

Connections: Builds on: Unit 0: How Science Works; 1-B Parts, Parents, and Young; 3.4 Survival, Fossils, and Change. Builds toward: Unit 7 Cells; Unit 9 Body Systems & Homeostasis; Unit 8 Classifying Life.
